concepts.explanation: Talking or stalling endlessly in the US Senate to block a vote. Ending one takes 60 of 100 senators.
Formal charges against an official by a legislature. It is the accusation, not removal; a trial follows.
Drawing voting district boundaries to favour one party.
Paid efforts to influence politicians' decisions on behalf of a company, industry or cause.
A directive from the US president that has the force of law without a vote in Congress.
The power to reject a law passed by the legislature.
Penalties such as trade bans or frozen assets used to pressure a country or person without military force.
A government formed by several parties sharing power because none won a majority alone.
A direct public vote on a single question rather than on candidates.
The US system where states, not the national popular vote, decide the president through allocated electors.
A meeting of party members to choose candidates or set policy. In some US states, it replaces a primary vote.
A vote to choose which candidate a party will put forward for the main election.
Someone who exposes wrongdoing inside an organisation, often at personal risk.
Arranging things so a leader can credibly claim not to have known about an action.
A parliamentary vote that, if lost, forces the government or leader to resign.
Rule by a leader or small group with strong central power and limited political freedom.
The senior group of ministers or secretaries who run government departments and advise the leader.
The government's chief lawyer and, in the US, head of the Justice Department.
A prosecutor appointed from outside normal channels to investigate a case with a conflict of interest.
The international body where countries negotiate; its Security Council can authorise sanctions or force.
